speechtext: I think he did a masterful job in re-enunciating and reaffirming all those principles which he stated so well at the FMC two weeks ago.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Those principles, of course, are consistent with the Government's desire to make sure that native people do much better than they did under 15 years of Liberal rule.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that answer is not really in the style of a Minister I have known since he was a very good mayor of Toronto. The Minister has referred to the last-minute bailout which was just issued at 1.30 by the Prime Minister. I am obviously invited by the Minister to address a question to the Prime Minister. He refers to that report as having been written by bureaucrats. Of course it was not written by bureaucrats.
The Deputy Prime Minister had a committee composed of outside business colleagues, most of whom were ideological friends of the Prime Minister. It was not a committee composed of bureaucrats at all.
In a salvage operation, the Prime Minister has appointed the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to supervise a committee to direct the future of the aboriginal peoples, something which is already the responsibility of the Minister. In other words, he is being asked to head a committee which is supervising the matter overseen by his own Department. Would the Prime Minister give the commitment that the recent Federal-Provincial Conference was not a sham in light of what has been happening in a clandestine fashion under the aegis of his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, I should say that that question is not in keeping with the style that the Right Hon. Member once exhibited as Minister of Finance some years ago. In point of fact we did not say that bureaucrats will do anything other than advise. The Government itself will make policy. There is nothing in here that said that the report-
They weren't bureaucrats.

I get the indulgence of my right hon. friend. It does not say that the report in question was prepared by bureaucrats. It was prepared by an outside advisory group. What I heard at the First Ministers' Conference on Aboriginal Peoples from the aboriginal peoples was this: "We have had it up to the teeth with the manner in which the federal Government has administered our lives over the last number of years and we want to listen to new ideas and new approaches that will benefit us and bring equality and justice to aboriginals across the country." We are simply saying that there may be some good ideas and, if they will benefit aboriginal peoples, we will listen to them and implement them in a spirit of fairness and decency.
Oh, oh!

Liberal Members should not be heckling the aboriginal peoples. They should be listening, because this is a vitally important question that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development addresses with great leadership and sensitivity at all times.
April 18, 1985

Mr. Speaker, while we are on the subject of new ideas and fresh approaches, I would like to put a question to the Prime Minister. As he probably knows, yesterday Norway very wisely and with some courage made a statement indicating that it would not become involved in star wars research. It has turned down the American invitation to do so.
It is clear that this Government's own sense of uncertainty is only causing dissension in the government caucus, and deep anxiety in the country. It is also losing a chance for Canada to make a very important and effective statement on the whole question of arms control and disarmament. Taking into account the stand Norway has taken, and the fact that the West Germans and the French are also developing a joint position, I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he would now join our NATO ally, Norway, and clearly indicate, in a very polite and direct way, that we, as a country, also do not intend to become involved in the research and development program that would lead to that very highly dangerous and destabilizing initiative of President Reagan.

Mr. Speaker, what we will do is what the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs set out with great clarity and dignity on January 21. We will support our friends and allies in regard to the research component of the concept inasmuch as the Geneva negotiations were weeks away from beginning. We will examine any other possibilities pursuant to the national interest of Canada.
We have received what has been referred to as an invitiation. We will make the necessary inquiries. We will take a look at it in Cabinet, and we will be guided by what we have done at the insistence of the Minister of National Defence, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and myself, when we included, for the first time, a sovereignty clause in our defence agreements. We will protect the sovereignty, independence, and integrity of Canada, and we shall always act in the national interest of this country, as a friend and loyal supporter of NATO, and as a believer in freedom, justice, and democracy.

Mr. Speaker, those are all values and purposes to which we can adhere. They key question is when will the Government make a decision in order to show us how it intends to keep those values.
I would ask the Prime Minister to confirm whether or not the country has now received an extension on that invitation from the United States, and whether or not there is some intention to send a task force composed only of Conservative Members of Parliament to Washington to discuss this matter with the Americans. I would like to get some kind of guarantee

from the Prime Minister that, if there is to be such a task force, it would be a task force involving all Members of the House because we represent all Canadians, and that any extension would not result in the Government making a decision after Parliament has closed, at which time it would not have to face Parliament with what is a very critical decision in the history of our country.

Mr. Speaker, this is coming from a Cabinet Minister who was a member of a Government that never once in its life ever brought a treaty to Parliament prior to signing it. It always signed them behind the backs of the Canadian people. He now has the temerity to rise and say what he has said.

Not true.

We will consider them and, pursuant to that, we will report to the House. I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs is deeply committed to consulting with opposition Parties and to keeping the House and the Canadian people fully involved in and informed of our intentions and actions in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
subtopic: STATEMENT ON TASK FORCE REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just tabled the response of the Government to the first report of the Task Force on parliamentary reform. I was very pleased to do so because my colleagues and I, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), have long held the view that the Government can only be a true instrument of the Canadian people if it is accountable to them through Parliament.
The Government was anxious to proceed with reform immediately following its election last fall. However, we recognized that Members of Parliament had to lead the effort for reform and that meaningful changes in the rules and structure of the House of Commons could only come about as a result of co-operation and consensus between members of all Parties. It was for that reason that the commitment to create a Task Force on the Reform of the House of Commons was outlined in the Speech from the Throne.
The members of the task force have taken their mandate to heart and produced a unanimous report which proposes significant changes to the rules of the House and the role of Members of Parliament. Therefore, I am pleased to tell the House that the Government supports the adoption of the majority of the task force's recommendations and we propose a trial period of one year in accordance with past practice with respect to the implementation of new and provisional rules.
As Members will know, reforms proposed in the last Parliament by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure formed the basis for the Provisional Standing Orders under which the House now functions. The Government believes that the recommendations contained in the first report complete the work undertaken by the special committee. For that reason, it is appropriate to adopt the recommendations contained in the first report of the task force at this time rather than waiting for a final report of the task force.
That having been said, the Government proposes to deal with all future reports of the task force as a package in order to avoid a piecemeal approach to parliamentary reform. As the final report of the task force is expected before the House adjourns for the summer recess, we believe this will not impose any delay in the reform effort.
Having outlined the general background, I would like to turn to a discussion of some of the specifics of those recommendations. The Government has noted its technical concerns about specific recommendations in the annex to the comprehensive response. In no instance have we found an obstacle that cannot be overcome. As you know, the task force has proposed that a change be made in the method of electing the occupant of the Chair. Although there is no reason to believe that there would be any need to elect a Speaker within the one-year trial period being recommended by the Government, we feel that this is an integral part of the reforms suggested by the task force and that the incorporation of this proposal in the experimental rules would send an important message to Members about our commitment to ensuring their increased participation in House affairs.

April 18, 1985

By agreeing to include Private Members and Members of the Opposition on the Board of Internal Economy, the Government will be asking Members to take responsibility for the management of the House of Commons, to meet the needs of Members and to make informed and accountable decisions about matters which impact upon public expenditures.
Independence in the management of the institution will be paralleled by an increased independence in the legislative operations of the House. The Government has and will continue to have the right and responsibility to initiate legislation, but Private Members must play a greater role in the legislative process. For example, we agree that the scheduling of Private Members' Business could more appropriately be done by the Table Officers than by the Government House Leader's office. Private Members should not feel that their right to initiate legislation is controlled by the Government or any Minister of that Government.
This is also the thrust of the recommendation that any four members of a House committee be permitted to initiate a meeting on due notice. In agreeing to adopt this proposal, the Government is taking a major step toward increasing real authority of the committees of the House.
More and more, the substantive work of Parliament will be done in its committees. By providing committees with greater independence and by increasing their budgets and staff resources, the Government hopes that Members of Parliament will apply their considerable skills not only to the study and improvement of legislation, but also to the analysis of major issues. When we create legislative committees, we will free the standing committees to devote their full time to the consideration of estimates, annual reports and special studies.
As well, it is the Government's hope that the removal of the automatic provision for questions of confidence on votable Supply motions will encourage the Opposition to bring forward substantive policy proposals for the consideration of the House.
Finally, we were pleased to see the recommendation that statements by Ministers be streamlined to ensure that time is not lost from the consideration of Government business. Contrary to the practice in recent years, this Government has made a conscientious effort to make major policy statements in the House and I believe there have been at least 20 occasions when major statements have been made by Ministers in the House. I might add that we have taken these steps at the expense of time which would have been available for Government business in the House. We believe the appropriate place to announce and debate policy is in the House, not, with the greatest of deference, in the National Press Theatre.
Since the task force report was tabled in the House, the Government has engaged in consultations with members of all Parties and a consensus in support of the task force recommendations has emerged. As I have said, the Government would like to see reforms introduced as a co-operative effort and I would like to thank my colleagues, particularly those in the Opposition, for the role they have played in this regard. The job is not finished. It is my intention to meet with the
House of Commons Reform
Opposition House Leaders in the very near future to discuss the timetable and method of implementation of the proposed reforms in accordance with the spirit that has prevailed up to this point with respect to consultation.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the Chairman-

Similarly, we do not see the need for a one-year experiment with regard to the composition of the Commissioners of Internal Economy. There is so great a consensus on adding Private Members, including Opposition Members, to the management council of the House of Com-

April 18, 1985
House of Commons Reform
mons that 1 cannot understand why any experiment should be necessary.
Most other parliamentary jurisdictions have adopted an all-Party approach to such matters, and I would not think that we would be well served by delaying a permanent solution as recommended by the task force. Let us do this as soon as possible by bringing forward permanent amendments to the legislation in question, because as we know this requires a legislative change rather than simply having to amend our Standing Orders.
We welcome also the acceptance of the recommendations regarding statements in the House. I would say to the President of the Privy Council, however, that this change will work only if he insists that his colleagues adhere rigorously to his regime of giving ample notice of the statement, as well as providing copies of it, to the Opposition critics well in advance. I know that the hon. gentleman has tried to persuade his colleagues to co-operate, but on a number of occasions they have not done so. I want to commend those Ministers who endeavour to make that system work, even when it is decided to give a statement only shortly before the House opens. 1 could give a bit of a report card on those who have made it work and those who have not, but I think those to whom I could refer will know who they are. This procedure will work only if Ministers will co-operate and only in this way will an increase in the use of Minister's statements in fact enhance the role of this House of Commons.
The small alteration in arranging Private Members' Business certainly is acceptable to the Official Opposition, but the suggestion by the Government that a failure to provide 24 hours' notice results in the loss of Private Members' Business lends itself too readily to manipulation by a Government wanting to find a few extra hours of Government time. It is not unknown after all for Government back-benchers to respond readily to the Ministry's suggestions, if not outright direction.
The most interesting changes, of course, will be with regard to committees. The provision of budgets and staff is long overdue, but Members should remember that this places more demands on them rather than fewer. We must guard against creating committee bureaucracies. They must be instruments, tools, of service to the Members of Parliament in their work, not their masters.
With respect to the proposals regarding changes in the committee system, I must say I personally have some questions and there are questions that could be raised about the concept of legislative committees. In a House the size of ours, I believe that specialized committees are best suited to dealing with legislation; but our Party is certainly willing to see how the recommendations for legislative committees work for a one-year trial period. I am quite concerned, however, that the Government is already trying to dilute the effectiveness of the experiment by not agreeing to make Ministers members of legislative committees on their own Bills. This is a very serious departure from the concept of legislative committees and makes me wonder how seriously the Government is really prepared to take Parliament in this important area. After all,
Mr. Speaker, there are already disturbing signs that Ministers of the current Government are not taking our current committees as seriously as they should when it comes to willingness to attend committee hearings, to stay at those hearings for the appropriate length of time and in fact to give due notice of when they are ready to come before a committee.
As far as dealing with tax bills in a committee other than a Committee of the Whole is concerned, I became convinced of the need for this many years ago when I had the responsibility of steering such matters through the House. I would hope that as far as possible most Ways and Means Bills would be considered in the same legislative committee because they are so interrelated.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to try and deal with all the recommendations but let me say that I welcome the willingness of the Government to try these experiments. I hope the Government will not succumb to any temptation to try to use the more complex committee system to diffuse the political process for its own objectives or to try to use the changes only to keep otherwise errant Government backbenchers busy. Most important, I hope all Members realize that these experimental rules mean more work, not less. New rules in themselves do not automatically make Parliament better; only the diligent work of Members can do that. In the meantime I await the call of the President of the Privy Council to discuss the details and terms of the proposed experiment.
I want to congratulate all members of the task force on their work. We await with interest their further reports and the Government's response to these reports.
This House of Commons and its committees are fundamental to the functioning, the very existence, of our democratic system of government. It is in the interest of all Canadians that we strive on an on-going basis to make the House and its committees as relevant and as effective as possible in terms of the needs of the country and its people. I believe the report will make a real contribution to achieving these objectives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by congratulating the committee. I know the hard work that went into the development of the report, both in the past and the report on which the committee is currently working.
I want to say something about the committee. The committee could well serve as a model for other committees. The way the committee has worked together, the way the committee has sought consensus, and the way the committee has worked in what I think could reasonably be described as a relatively non-partisan way I hope will be an example for the committees that will flow from the report we have before us here today.
There is no question that Parliament will be effectively changed by the recommendations being adopted which the Government House Leader indicated the Government is will-
April 18, 1985

ing to see implemented here today. We are going to see Parliament move from what has been a somewhat misunderstood institution, I suspect, into a reasonably modern age. With the change, however, there will be a shift in the focus of Parliament.
While much of the focus of Parliament, from a public point of view, has been here in the House of Commons until now, with the new committee structure, funding arrangements and staffing arrangements that will be made available, a lot of the work that previously was done here will now be done by the committees. Therefore, the public of Canada will also have to adjust to the changed focus of Parliament. In addition, if the committees do in fact take their lead from the special committee's example and if the chairmen of the committees that will be established can take their lead from the work of the chairman of this committee, I am confident that the work of Parliament will be enhanced by the recommendations being adopted.
Like many Members, I am somewhat apprehensive, but nevertheless willing to go ahead with the change. It was our view that this committee, having worked as it did, deserved to see its recommendations implemented. We ought not to adjust unecessarily any of the recommendations. It may well be that the question of having Ministers as members of committees studying their legislation is something that will require additional thought. Although the Government has indicated that perhaps it is not prepared to proceed with that change, after our discussions maybe there will be a way to incorporate it in the final recommendation that will become legislation and will become part of the temporary rules of the House of Commons come September of this year. It is to that that I want to address myself.
It is very important, now that we have the Government's response-a response which I might say I welcome and a response which I might say is pleasantly surprising-that we set about to work out the methods of implementation. We do not have a lot of time. The rules will have to be in place by this summer in order that those who are going to have the responsibility for administering, whether it be the Table Officers, the Speaker, the committee chairmen or the administration of the House of Commons, will have time to become fully aware of the changes that have taken place and to put in place the mechanisms necessary to allow for the changes to be effective.
For example, the request for ways to ensure adequate funding for committees will have to receive serious discussion about how that will take place, what methods will be used to determine budgets and who will be responsible for the final decisions on matters such as that. Therefore, those things must be put in place very quickly.
The other matter that strikes me as making very much sense is the proposal to include opposition Members among those who administer the House of Commons. It is quite clear that, since the Commissioners of Internal Economy deal primarily with matters relating to those things directly responsible to Parliament, Parliament itself has to be represented on that, all of Parliament and not just simply the Government side. There-
House of Commons Reform
fore, I welcome the proposal from the committee in the first place and the Government's acceptance of the proposal to establish a place for the Opposition.
I trust that the recommendation will be interpreted in such a way as to make sure that both opposition Parties will be represented. I would certainly find myself somewhat less supportive if that were not to be the case. For example, I would not like to see members of the Liberal Party left out. I want them there.

Member will know, we had an unprecedented occasion on which all three House Leaders, arm in arm, cheek by jowl, shoulder to shoulder appeared before the task force. One of the things upon which we all agreed, I think, is that in accordance with the tradition that we have established, we should implement these matters on a provisional basis for a period of one year to iron out the kinks so that we can in fact review these matters at the end of that period of time and make improvements after we have had the benefit of experience.

April 18, 1985
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the warm-up just before the luncheon break, I was addressing the central principle and purpose of this legislation, which is to provide for a response to one of the fundamental responsibilities within the federal Government-to ensure a fair sharing of equity across Canada in terms of the distribution of benefits and certainly the distribution of economic opportunities. I was making the case that one of the serious transgressions and uncertainties which has become the hallmark of the recent Government is its lack of attention and sensitivity to those issues, and that in fact the whole thrust of its economic program is not a thrust at all, but a scattered, disorganized, chaotic, random set of actions which has no coherence as far as a regional development program is concerned. We only have to return to the November 8 statement for proof of that. It is recognized that those areas which are most disadvantaged suffer the most severely by federal government cut-backs. There is a direct relationship and axiom between the two. The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) has become one of the alltime slashers of history. In fact, it is a deliberate attack upon the regional foundations of Canada. We saw a clear example of this today in Question Period. His advisory committee was given the objective of trying to reduce the deficit and in fact chose an area of programming dealing with economic benefits for native people. That is the choice which it made as the basis for its so-called reduction. Once again, those least able to protect themselves and those most in need of economic opportunity will be the victims of this peculiar and ill-thought-out approach to economic matters in Canada.
Certainly we see it not only in the cut-backs in industrial development programs, in investments in public infrastructure, in transportation, in research and in the environment, but we see it, perhaps most seriously, in the erosion of other forms of transfer programs.
I should like to talk about one program in particular, the unemployment insurance program. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has made it quite clear that he intends to transfer a large proportion of the present premium rate of unemployment insurance back to the tax rolls. This means that the unemployment insurance program, which probably nets a full $2 billion of transfers to the poorer regions of Canada to ensure at least some basic level of income stability, will not be subject to entitlements under the Unemployment Insurance Act, but to the whims and caprices of the Minister of Finance and his officials at tax time. In fact, we will see a total erosion of the program. We have already seen cut-backs in severance pay and on pension rights. Who does that hurt? It is not the well-to-do nor the members of the "Mulroney Club". It hurts people who are faced with economic disadvantage. Those are the ones who are affected by those kinds of cuts, not the friends of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who are paying a hundred dollars for special access and special privilege. The ones who are really being hurt are those in the region.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I see Conservative Members are coming to life. I suppose it is because they are not members of the club. They went through that awkward stage of getting themselves elected as Members of Parliament only to find out it is really the people who can afford it who get special access to the Prime Minister. That is the way the system works. I give my deep sympathies to members of that caucus that they have been so excluded from the privileged circle of access and information, but that is something that they will have to work out for themselves.
The point I am making is that this attempt by the Government to build one block upon another has become a major withdrawal of commitments to regional development. In my own Province of Manitoba the evidence is very clear. As a result of the November 8 statement, the minimum reduction of job levels in that province was 4,000 permanent jobs, to say nothing of the 2,000 summer jobs which were lost. That is clearly reflected in the substantially increased unemployment statistics for that province. The withdrawal of federal investment in a number of important projects, the slowing down of the Churchill program, the withdrawal from the rebuilding of the railway cars at Transcona, the stoppage of the downtown programs, are all beginning to eat into the responsibility of the federal Government to invest in regions which do not have the economic wherewithal. Now Government has added insult to injury by bringing in on top of that a further reduction in the equalization payments. The two-year program which is announced in this Bill in fact will result in approximately a $60 million reduction according to the figures which were provided by the Minister of Finance himself; some $22 million in this fiscal year and some $37 million in the next fiscal year.
I go back to my point and the point which was raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gar-neau), who argued that the equalization is so essential an underpinning to the whole question of regional equity and regional sharing, that it should not be one which is arbitrarily decided by this Government alone. Surely, in the spirit of co-operation and consultation and all the fine sounding promises which were made, this is an area which should certainly be discussed, but it was not. There was no agreement with the provinces. They were simply handed a fait accompli. The only access to information they had is when the Minister of Finance left his briefing books on a coffee table in a Winnipeg hotel. That was the only way they found out what the Department of Finance and the Minister were really thinking. That is a very unique and curious way to transfer information back to the provinces. It certainly saves on stamps, but the fact is that it does not result in the kind of sharing of information which is essential to make this kind of program work.
If one looks at the various tiers of assistance, one finds the withdrawal of direct grants by the federal Government in terms of investment in federal programs. If one looks at the transfer programs to individuals such as unemployment insurance, one finds withdrawal. If one looks at the basic fiscal transfer programs, one finds withdrawal. 1 would suggest to
April 18, 1985

you, Mr. Speaker, that the total equation cannot be added up simply by taking a look at one tier. We have to look at the entire set of withdrawals, and we find that the poor regions of this country are becoming the real victims of the so-called economic renewal. And to be a so-called winner or loser in this society really depends upon where one lives and which kind of club one belongs to and whether one can afford it.
I also want to say, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces themselves cannot absolve themselves entirely of responsibility in this matter. I believe one of the most useful reports, one which has been dropped like a hot potato by the Government because it provides too much incriminating evidence on its friends, is a report on the funding of post-secondary education across Canada. It points out that over a period of time the federal transfers for post-secondary education were going up on an average of 13 per cent each year, and the provinces were not in any way matching those transfers. In fact, in my own Province of Manitoba in 1977-78, the proportion of funding for operating grants to provincial colleges and universities by the federal Government was 80 per cent. By 1984-85, it had reached 103 per cent. That example is repeated in several other provinces. I know that there have been provincial Governments, mainly Tory in origin, which have banged the table and said they were getting a raw deal. The fact is that these figures clearly point out that what was happening was that the federal Government was doing more than its share. In no way were those funds being matched by the provincial Governments. As a result, federal funds were in fact supplementing or subsidizing other provincial expenditures. It would seem to me that one of the clear priorities of the Minister of Finance must be a direct response to the facts and figures provided in this report. This report demonstrates dramatically how the provincial Governments have been camouflaging in terms of fair sharing.
We are not saying that the federal Government, when it gets into questions related to fiscal arrangements between the provinces and the federal Government, should simply put more money on the table. But it should at least adopt some kind of bargaining attitude. It should at least come together with a total package in mind. What is it going to do on higher education? What is it going to do on unemployment insurance or regional development grants? That is the kind of effective federal-provincial initiative which we would recommend and which my colleague who spoke first in this debate strongly promoted and endorsed.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, to Hon. Members opposite that they should recognize that this is one of the vital issues with which they will have to deal. If they fail to come up with a clear, concise and coherent answer and response to the question of how to deal with regional inequities, and fail to make sure that federal and provincial Governments share equally in the responsibilities in that area, we will have a serious problem down the road in not being able to provide for proper economic opportunities for all Canadians. Once we are in that situation, the very basic underpinnings and foundations of this country are in danger.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-39, an Act to provide for the making of supplementary fiscal equalization payments to certain provinces for the period April 1, 1982 to March 31, 1987, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that every time I have the opportunity to speak in the House, you are in the chair, so I hope I will keep you interested today, as I have tried to in the past.
I would first like to commend the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and her colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), for bringing forward Bill C-39. On behalf of my constituents and those Manitobans who feel we finally found a Government which recognized equalization payments were not the size they should be, I thank the Minister and the Government for the extra $115 million Manitoba will receive in the next two years. This Bill is an example of the fairness and good will which our Government has with respect to the provinces and to our country. It is also an example of the way our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wants to see a fair and reasonable Government, and I commend the Government for taking the action it has taken in this particular Bill.
It is always interesting to see how the Opposition handles good legislation. I listened to the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) and the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). The Hon. Member for Churchill stood up and thanked the Minister for part of the money and then proceeded to try to pat the NDP on the back by saying that Manitoba got more money becauses of the NDP Government and the NPD Members in the House of Commons. He said:
Mr. Speaker, I should first say that, unlike hon. members of the New Democratic Party who spend a lot of time crowing but get little action out of the noise they make, hon. members of the Conservative Party who reside in and represent Manitoba, have constantly dealt with me on a quiet basis on this issue. I can tell the Hon. Member that they were far more effective in their representations because they had substance and a good analytical basis for the statements they made, as opposed to the shrill rhetoric we received from the other Party.
1 think that says it in a nutshell. It is not necessary to get up in this House and bombard us with rhetoric.

I want to commend the Minister for bringing forward the Bill at this time. It is good legislation. It is fair legislation. I hope the House will see fit to pass it so we can obtain Royal Assent so that the provinces who need this assistance will have use of that money this year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I say what I had intended to say, I would like to remark on the most recent comments of the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) who referred to the deficit in Manitoba solely within the category of spending. In the interests of intellectual honesty, the Member for Winnipeg-St. James ought to acknowledge that the deficit in Manitoba, as is the case with deficits in all the provinces in the country and in the federal Government, has as much to do with a shortfall in revenue due to the economic recession which we have just come through, as it has to do with government spending. Yet, we continue to hear this kind of rhetoric about spending from Conservative Members of Parliament, Conservative Governments, and Conservative MLAs, to the extent that one begins to wonder what kind of simple view they have of economics which allows them to talk about increased deficits without making distinctions between revenue shortfalls and increased government spending and between what money is and is not being spent on. The world is much more complicated than the Member for Winnipeg-St. James would have us believe. Perhaps the reason is that he and his colleagues do not realize the complexity of the issue. However, if they are going to speak about deficits they should take that into consideration.
Members, particularly those from the Conservative Party, should also talk about the balanced books that were left to the Progressive Conservatives who took over government in Saskatchewan in 1982. Conservative Members never recount the history of the balanced Budget in Saskatchewan and the fact that a Progressive Conservative administration not only suffered a general revenue shortfall after taking office in that province, as all Governments suffered as a result of economic conditions, but created a deliberate revenue shortfall by proceeding with its ludicrous promises about reducing certain taxes.
That province had a history of impeccable fiscal responsibility. It now has a deficit in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James could have mentioned that in his remarks, but it would not have lent credence to his argument.
Let me deal specifically with the Bill which introduces supplementary equalization payments. I would like to share with Members who are present and those people who may be watching some of the history of this regime. I recall the time when Bill C-97 was introduced by the former Liberal Government. The intention of that Bill was to establish a unilateral change in equalization payments.
I represented my Party in the committee that studied that Bill. At that time I collaborated with the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) who I believe moved a motion which 1 seconded in a rare moment of unanimity between the Hon. Member and myself. We have subsequently had occasion to agree with respect to the Canada Health Act, but with respect to Bill C-97, in a rare moment of unanimity the Hon. Member moved a motion, which I seconded, calling for an amendment to Bill C-97 which would have had the effect of doing what the Government is only partially accomplishing now, that is, restoring that money to Manitoba. Both the Hon. Member for Provencher and I felt at that time that that money rightfully belonged to Manitoba but that it was being deprived of it as a result of that Bill.
Immediately after the election on September 4, I wrote to the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare to remind him of our collaboration in 1982 and to ask him if he would use his influential position as a Cabinet Minister in the new Government to ensure that Manitoba had its $72 million restored.
It took a great deal of time for the Government to announce this legislation and many people were involved in bringing it forward. The Manitoba Government should receive a lot of credit for its persistence in insisting that the federal Government come up with that money. I believe that I can say with absolute assurance that this legislation would not be before us today if there were a Progressive Conservative Government in Manitoba, because that administration would have been silent in the interest of Party unity and federal-provincial relations. It would have had very little to say about the injustice being done to Manitoba.
However, as a result of there being an NDP Government in Manitoba, it was able to stand up to the federal Government and demand justice for our province. As a result of that stand over the last six months we are able to speak to this legislation today.
This legislation comes about also as a result of the efforts of many Manitobans who wrote to their Members of Parliament, to Progressive Conservative Members in the Cabinet, and who wrote in support of the Manitoba Government's position to let it be known that the federal Government should take action to redress the situation that was visited upon Manitoba unilaterally by the Liberals in 1982.
This legislation will provide in the first year $50 million to Manitoba of the $72 million which everyone believes is owed
April 18, 1985

to the Government. However, as the provincial Government has said and we have said, we welcome this action. While we are not satisfied completely, it is a response to a perceived injustice, and the Government should be commended to a degree for doing that. No one has disputed that fact but the history of the situation should be understood.
The only people who cannot take any credit for this are the Liberals. They originally brought about that unilateral injustice. I notice there are none of them present in the House.

speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, if I was inaccurate in my remarks. I did not notice the Hon. Member at the front of the House.
In any event, it is only the Liberal Party of Canada that cannot take any political satisfaction from what is happening today because it is they who unilaterally brought about the injustice that is being partially corrected in this legislation. They are the ones who remained silent, for all intents and purposes, during the time when Manitobans of every political stripe were trying to persuade the federal Government to move in this respect.
I might say that it took some time to gain the support of some Manitobans. I am thinking of the Progressive Conservative Leader of the Opposition in Manitoba, Mr. Filmon. Although he aspires to be the Premier of the province, at that point, at least, he knew nothing of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. At that time he was so naive as to suggest that the Manitoba Government had somehow agreed to this unilateral reduction. He did not know what he was talking about and I am sure he was advised of his mistake. Perhaps it was the Hon. Member for Provencher who had to tell him that this reduction in equalization payments for Manitoba was a unilateral action by the Liberals which the Conservatives as well as the Manitoba Government opposed at the time.
In fact, the Manitoba Government in the person of Vic Schroeder, the Minister of Finance, appeared before the committee to oppose that legislation. I am sure that Mr. Filmon was asked not to go around the province saying that the Manitoba Government agreed to that action because it would have been an embarrassment to the Conservatives to see that he did not know what he was talking about.
Some time later, the Leader of the Opposition in Manitoba must have been advised of the facts of the case and how this had really come about. Ultimately, Manitoba was able to present a united front with respect to the need for the federal Government to take this action.
I hope that background will be of assistance to those who want to know exactly what took place with respect to this issue and I hope that this legislation is an indication from the new
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments
Government that it intends fully to respect the principle of equalization which is enshrined in our Constitution.
I believe that a number of improvements can be made to equalization, some of which were recommended by the special Task Force on Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements which reported in 1981 and on which I had an opportunity to serve. Those recommendations included an enriched equalization arrangement for those provinces that fall below a certain economic criterion. There are a number of other recommendations in that report concerning equalization that I would commend to the House for further study.
We know that in 1987 these will come up for renewal. I have suggested to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that he recommend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that perhaps Parliament should be involved in this review again, as it was prior to 1982, although the procedure did not work at that time because the Government operated unilaterally. However, there was a special parliamentary task force dealing with federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. Perhaps Members from all Parties should again be involved in a review of those arrangements. That might be a tradition well worth establishing and it would become a tradition if we did it again in anticipation of the 1987 agreement.
I hope the Government will give serious consideration to that recommendation which I am making now and which 1 have made before.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this discussion and in particular to reply to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) to the effect that the provision concerning the eligibility of the spouses allowance is too restrictive.

April 18, 1985
Spousal Allowance
Ideally, the program should indeed go a step further, and I am quite willing to admit that the allowance will not be available to everyone. However, Mr. Speaker, the Government has to face the economic and social realities. One of those economic facts is the unprecedented deficit that the Government budget has been plagued with. This Government must therefore proceed with caution and try to alleviate that burden by implementing sound economic policies as well as promoting a responsible social and financial development.
It would of course, be irresponsible to promise funds when we are short of money. It would also be irresponsible for the Government not to make a commitment to share the funds available. So, Mr. Speaker, we took the only approach that was both responsible and cautious to that reform: we made a commitment to use the scarce resources available to help those people in our society who are most in need of help and protection. In other words, the spouse's allowance be extended to all needy widows and widowers between 50 and 64, regardless of the spouse's age at the time of death. Finally, this amendment will allow us to include in the spouse's allowance program those Canadians who have been left out since of the legislation was first implemented. And in my opinion, this proposal and the related increase are no different from most proposals put before the House of Commons.
In fact, a large part of the social legislation introduced in the House aims at improving social benefits gradually. Each amendment adds a little to the security net by extending the eligibility, increasing the allowances and adjusting the programs according to changing social realities.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the spouse's allowance program, like the old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement, has developed gradually thanks to several improvements made to the original provisions. It is a well known fact, known even to the Members of this House. In fact, by the mere implementation of the guaranteed income supplement in 1967, the government of the day recognized that the basic old age security pension in itself did not provide an adequate income to people without any other source of income, more particularly if the additional income that future pensioners might expect under the newly implemented Canada Pension Plan were taken into account. The supplement subject to a means test was thus introduced to help the neediest pensioners.
However, the shortcomings of this supplement soon became apparent. In 1971, to take into account the various situations and needs of pensioners, both single and married, different and more adequate rates were introduced for the guaranteed income supplement.
As the economic situation evolved, it became obvious that the original provision limiting the indexation to 2 per cent inadequate to the extent that the purchasing power of the aged was being increasingly eroded. Therefore, in 1972 and 1973, more realistic provisions came into effect for quarterly increases in the allowances in line with the rise in the consumer price index. The progress of the supplement did not stop there. The monthly supplement paid to a couple of pensioners was increased by $20 in 1979 and by $35 in 1980.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that this House and its Members have sometimes been accused of going around in circles. I must admit that there is a certain truth to the allegation. In 1984, we took measures to correct once again an injustice in the level of allowances paid to couples with only one pensioner as opposed to couples with both spouses being pensioners. In fact, in the first case, an increase of $50 was granted. Finally, new Canadians will be entitled to a basic minimum income equal to the allowance paid to Canadians who have been in the country for a long time.
I mention these amendments merely to prove without the shadow of a doubt that this Government has absolutely nothing to brag about because it proposed an approach based on progressive increases to enhance social programs. Indeed, the spouse allowance which we are discussing today was introduced to compensate for the shortcomings of the Old Age Security Program and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, for if the benefits paid under these programs were enough for couples where both spouses were pensioners or for single pensioners, they were simply inadequate in providing decent assistance to couples where only one of the spouses was a pensioner.
The allowance was therefore introduced in 1975, subject to a means test, to assist needy spouses aged 60 to 64 of old age security pensioners. It is a fact that thousands of needy spouses have been helped.
Unfortunately, the allowance was cancelled when the pensioner died. Thus, the spouse would lose not only the income of the pensioner, but also his or her own allowance, at a time when he or she actually most needed this assistance, when he or she was the most unable to cope with the situation.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, the safety net was made a little wider. In 1979, when our Party came to power, provisions were made to extend the allowance after the death of the pensioner until the surviving spouse reached age 65 or remarried.
In 1979, in 1980 and 1984, the spouse allowance program was again enhanced, more specifically by bringing in the same improvements as in the case of the Guaranteed Income Supplement, so that the allowance recipients would be treated equitably.
I think that I have established clearly that our proposal to extend spouse allowance eligibility to needy widows and widowers aged 60 to 64 is another step in the evolution of the program. Of course, we would prefer being able to help a greater number of needy Canadians, but the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) is only too well aware that what is preventing us from doing so is the extremely
April 18, 1985

disastrous financial situation in which we found ourselves on September 5.
The Hon. Member says that we are curbing the allowance granted to this group of needy Canadians, while we are actually extending eligibility to this group. While he has stated that we are excluding those who will not be entitled to the allowance, 1 would say that we are including those who will become eligible. Finally, while he says that we are penalizing those who will not be eligible, I say that we are offering long-awaited assistance to needy widows and widowers aged 60 to 64.
Mr. Speaker, if we analyze the comments made by the Hon. Member, we could summarize them as follows: If you cannot do everything, do not do anything. This approach may be defended in theory, but in actual practice, it results in inactivity and failure to help. For my part, I believe that we should be proud of doing our best at this time when we have the opportunity to do so.
In closing, I would like to quote these words from Cicero: "Let us be guided by reason rather than by public opinion."

However, before going any further, I would like to make one thing very clear. The government is not limiting the eligibility to the spouses allowance, on the contrary, despite our own very serious financial position at this time we are proposing for the first time ever to extend to all low-income widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64 the protection offered by this important social program.
The spouses allowance, Mr. Speaker, is the monthly amount that is now paid to low-income spouses between the ages of 60 and 64 of old-age security pensioners, or to widows or widowers of old-age pensioners who were entitled to it at the time the pensioners died.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there are two different categories of needy people between the ages of 60 and 64 who get a guaranteed minimum income under the Spouse's Allowance Program. First, the spouses of guaranteed income supplement recipients, and second, the widows and widowers over 60 who were eligible to the allowance when the pensioned spouse died.
It is obvious that the Spouse's Allowance Program as it exists today leaves something to be desired. People in the same age group as the allowance recipients, for whom the cost of living is just as high, are still not entitled to an allowance. Are we to believe that the then government made a mistake when it
Spousal Allowance
established the program in 1975? Did the succeeding governments err in broadening the initial conditions of eligibility to the program? Unlike some people, I would be prepared to undertake a task although I might not be certain to see it through. Fortunately, many of the architects of the Canadian social security system did not wait for such certainty before they acted.
Mr. Speaker, I have read over with care the debates that took place some years ago and to which my hon. colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) participated, concerning the necessary changes to be made to the Widows' allowances and the Old Age Security Pensions, and with that knowledge, I realize that the criticisms were always the same. When it comes to improving a program, it is advisable to go all the way. I believe this is an important step. On the other hand, considering the determination of my hon. colleague in defending this proposition and this motion, I found it amusing to see the kind of accusations brought against Members of the Opposition who were also asking for changes. They were told that if they wanted some changes it was because they had an ulterior motive, being recipients of the Old Age Security Pension.

The Old Age Security Program was going to be improved many times over the years: for instance, as my hon. colleague has just mentioned, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, an allowance based on a means test, was introduced in 1967 and the Spouse's Allowance, in 1975.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that I spent more than a few minutes on the history of Old Age Security. In fact, the development of the program is similar to that of the Spouse's Allowance. A program that, initially, was far from being perfect was extended and made more generous over the years, as succeeding governments considered they could spend additional resources on it.
What we must ask ourselves is this: Should we stop trying to improve the Old Age Security Program until we can afford to make it perfect? Must the Government refrain from helping those it can help on the pretence that it cannot for the time being improve the lot of other needy persons? Certainly not! We must continue to seek steady financial and social improvements whenever and however we can. And in this respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind my hon. colleague that the pension reform as proposed by the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is in line with the commitments we made during the last election. We are indeed too often blamed for not keeping our word.
And I also remember how vigorously at times that promise has been said to be ridiculous, that it did not make sense and yet, today there are people who say that not only does it make sense but that it should be extended. Like I said, in taking this step now we are moving in accordance with our promises and our means.
Another point was also important in terms of universality: Pensionable age could be lowered from 65-my hon. colleague knows that, it was also part of their political commitment- from 65 to 64 years of age. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the motion presented by the Liberal Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) concerning Bill C-26. The purpose of this Bill is to extend the Spouse's Allowance Program to all widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64, regardless of the age of their spouse at the time of death.
Spousal Allowance
This, Mr. Speaker, is a very significant step in the battle against poverty since this age group is particularly affected. Women in this age group are rarely poor as a result of misfortune or other foreseeable events. For the majority, their poverty is the consequence of the role society has assigned to them, their difficulty in gaining access to the job market, the conditions they have had to work under if they did work, and the poor protection they have had under the Canadian pension system.
Society has assigned the responsibility for rearing children and doing unpaid domestic work to women and the responsibility for meeting families' economic needs to men. People of my generation will remember the social disapproval there was in the past of any married woman, but particularly those with children, who wanted to get a paid job. Most working wives then were forced on to the labour market by the difficulty of their family's economic situation. Since the role society has reserved for women went hand in hand with financial dependency, it is not surprising that they are without resources when their husbands die.
The low level of participation in the labour market by older women also contributes to their poverty. According to Statistics Canada figures, only 26.2 per cent of women between the ages of 60 and 64 were in the workforce in 1984. Women of all ages made up 53.5 per cent of the workforce at that time.
This low figure may be explained by the many obstacles older women face when they try to get into, or go back into, the workforce after spending a large portion of their lives at home. First, there is the problem of training. What they have learned is often either obsolete or inadequate for the increasingly specialized needs of today. There are training and refresher courses available to prepare them for entry into the job market, but those cannot keep up with the demand. Older women must also face certain prejudices when it comes to candidate selection. A number of employers prefer to hire younger people over those who will be taking retirement in a few years. It is a well known fact that employability decreases as a person gets older.
Access to paid employment does not necessarily mean that women will be protected against poverty. Some who do work do so under the most unenviable conditions. They are still concentrated in a limited number of often poorly paid jobs with the least advantageous working conditions.
The protection offered to surviving spouses under the Canadian pension system is another cause of the difficult economic situation a large number of widows aged 60 to 64 find themselves in. I would remind you that in the Throne Speech the Government announced its intent to engage in discussions with the provinces on a total review of the Canadian pension system. Survivor benefits will be among the points discussed.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, those aged 60 to 64 deserve a better fate than the one in store for them at the present time. It is the duty of the Government to come to their assistance, regardless of the current economic situation. We are assuming that responsibility by proposing an extention of the Spouse's

April 18, 1985
Spousal Allowance
Allowance Program to all widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. Starting this coming September, some 85,000 people, 72,000 of them women, will be able to benefit from this measure. These 85,000 represent some 61 per cent of the total population of widows and widowers aged 60 to 64.
Essentially what we are offering to those people is the possibility of sufficient income to meet their basic needs. The Spouse's Allowance Program will guarantee them the same level of income as is currently provided to the surviving spouse of the pensioner who was in receipt of Old Age Security benefits before his death. At the moment, the maximum benefit is $536.26 per month. This figure will, however, be raised slightly in September since benefits are indexed every three months to the cost of living.
The Government is well aware that certain groups of the needy near-elderly will still be excluded from the Spouse's Allowance Program, but unfortunately we cannot go any further at this time given the current economic situation.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I express my sincere wish that the evolution of women's roles within society, the improvement of their working conditions, and the review of the Canadian pension system will mean that coming generations of women will be better off.

So, I was saying that it was necessary to find, as my colleague from the Conservative Party who spoke just before me has said, a way to rehabilitate these women in society and a small number of men as well, because more and more, we find couples where the man is the surviving spouse, and since his wife contributed a lot to the household revenue, once he reaches a certain age, he finds himself in the same situation as many women. So, I would like, as my colleague has said, this whole question of the quality of life for all senior Canadians be reviewed. Tonight, at six o'clock, I must leave to attend a dinner of the Gerontology Institute, in Hull, where the Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Bertrand) is scheduled to speak on this very subject of the quality of life of senior Canadians. She will address, I am confident, other aspects, apart from ways to alleviate current problems. She will speak about the future of Canadians, of those who are now on the labour market or, even, of those who just entered the labour market because it will take at least two or three decades before the situation described by my conservative colleague can change. When it does change, a woman will not have to totally depend on a man to survive, a woman will be paid the same as a man and, when she will reach a certain age and have to retire or cannot work anymore, she will be able to enjoy a fair revenue, a revenue above the poverty level and maybe even better if we have the chance to ensure the economic renewal which will allow us to improve the living conditions of all Canadians including our elderly.
Then, for example, there is the situation of people who are forced to retire. Many of our elderly live in poverty because, during their working life, they received a pay cheque which was maybe small, but was nevertheless large enough for their needs. They reach the age of 65 without any pension, because it is only recently that people have private pensions or they simply live on only the Government pension which, naturally, is not enough to give Canadians the same quality of life they enjoyed when they were on the labour market. Thus, forced retirement creates economic problems.
On the other hand, there is also the case, naturally, of people who would like to retire at 50 or 55. There is always a debate between these two groups of Canadians, the ones who would like to continue to work and receive the same revenue and the ones who think that once one has reached a certain age
April 18, 1985

and worked very hard for 30 or 40 years, maybe as a labourer, one should be able to retire. Therefore, those people should enjoy full retirement benefits and not get, as it is the case now, one third or one half of their pension if they retire before the compulsory limit of 65 years of age.
Retirement and sufficient income for people who would choose early retirement are all matters that need to be examined.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I commend the Hon. Member for his deep generosity, but I would like to hear from him a real commitment to participating in any review on compulsory retirement for Canadians. I suggest that he considers the means to provide sufficient income for senior citizens so that they become more financially independent than they are now. In the past, 35 workers supported one individual unable to work. Today, that equation is three workers for each individual who is either too young, too old, handicapped or too ill to work. And according to statistics, that proportion could fall to one worker having to support one other person unable to work. Perspectives in that area are such that one must obviously encourage and help Canadians to secure now income for their old days so they could lead an independent life without being a burden for the government.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for this opportunity to speak on that subject.

subtopic: HOUSING (A) DECISION TO CUT BUDGET FOR HOUSING RENOVATION PROGRAM. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT GIVE SUPPLEMENTARY FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when Conservative Members start talking about social issues, they really do not know what they are talking about. They do not have a clue! In March I had a question for the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), who is responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Mr. Speaker, after listening to the answers he gave me then, I said quite honestly that he did not know anything about the issue and that he was not even interested. And he knew even less about Quebec.
I think all Members of this House understand the importance of housing cooperatives and subsidized housing. There are three forms of subsidized housing. There is public housing, called HLM in Quebec or low-rent housing, which is financed by the provincial governments through the municipalities. We have non-profit organizations that are involved in residential construction and administered by a board consisting of five, seven or nine members. We have co-operatives whose members are all involved in carrying out the project.
To set up housing co-operatives, the Government finances interest payments. Co-operatives also help renew the supply of accommodation in working class neighbourhoods like in Sainte-Marie, and in towns across the country, where there are older homes that have to be renovated or restored. Usually, there are housing co-operatives organized by the tenants themselves. To help these people on moderate and low incomes to achieve something they would never be able to do without this formula, and become, collectively, the owners of their homes, they were allowed to take part in the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the RRAP.
A budget of about $5 million was allocated strictly to setting up non-profit housing co-operatives. This made it possible to reduce rental costs, to get decent housing and to help people on moderate and low incomes become homeowners.
Unfortunately, when I asked the question, the Minister wondered whether he was going to maintain this RRAP program and the $5 million it needs to upgrade housing through housing co-operatives.
The Minister was certainly faced with a very serious decision, but he is to blame for not having the guts to make his case with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) so he would not slack millions of dollars from the financing of social housing programs and the budget of the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, or RRAP. He kept silent in his chair and let the Minister of National Defence get all the money he wanted and left his own budgets truncated. However, the Parliamentary Secretary will be responding to my question later on, and I would like to tell him that I myself was parliamentary Secretary before September 4, and I trust that he will not just read the text prepared by his officials and will give us a satisfactory answer and tell us whether CMHC or the Minister have reached a decision and whether the financing of housing co-operatives under the RRAP program will be abolished or maintained. I would like him to tell us how many housing units will be cut off the programs this year. The figure is 5,000 units in the area of social housing. I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to give us specific answers to these questions. I trust that he is aware of the impact of the decision made by the Minister and CMHC. If he cuts back the budget of the RRAP program for housing co-operatives, these will disappear all across the country because this will result in rent increases and people will no longer be able to form co-operatives or non-profit organizations to invest in existing housing.
Social housing programs that do not come under the responsibility of provincial or municipal governments will apply only to the building of new housing, and we all know how costly new housing is and this means that the rents will be too high for some people.
Mr. Speaker, I see that the time at my disposal is nearly over and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will prove to be much more efficient than his Minister and will provide me with the answer to two questions: in the first place, has the Conservative Government decided to withdraw altogether the $5 million allocated the RRAP for housing co-operatives? Secondly, by how much will the number of housing units be reduced? The Parliamentary Secretary is aware that, in previous years, 25,000 housing units were built in Canada. How many units has the Government decided to cut back?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to respond to the matters raised in the House by the Hon. Member on March 14 of this year and the matters he has raised today. These matters concern the non-profit Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the co-operative housing program.
With respect to the co-operative housing program, CMHC has put in place a competitive process. The intent of this process is to review projects, whether they be submitted by co-ops or non-profit groups, in an equitable and fair manner. The procedure is based on objective selected criteria. The selection process has been designed to improve the degree to which federal assistance is directed to those most in need and to reduce the over-all costs through the selection of well targeted modest proposals on a competitive basis. This reflects the Minister's commitment to help people most in need of assistance and to ensure that available funds are used effectively.
At this stage in the selection process, more than 50 per cent or more than half the projects selected to proceed to the next selection stage or decision stage are indeed co-ops. The important consideration here is that co-ops are being treated in a fair manner. Co-ops are able to compete for subsidy units on an equal basis with other worthy groups. In this House the Minister has put the process in its proper prospective, reminding the Hon. Member that such project decisions are a func-
April 18, 1985

tion of CMHC's competitive process and not, I repeat, not a matter of ministerial preference.
With respect to the non-profit RRAP program, I am pleased to say that funding will be available in 1985 for those projects which are successful in the current competitive project selection process. Non-profit RRAP funds will be used in specified circumstances to ensure project viability. The emphasis will be on the need to overcome to the extent that it is possible project viability problems in those market areas where existing housing activity is essential to meet the identified housing needs of the country.
The Minister is indeed sensitive to the housing needs of the country and to any cut-backs that may be considered or put forward by various groups. The Minister is dedicated to providing a sound, reasonable housing policy directed to those most in need and he will continue to be so dedicated in the years ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up the question I put to the Government today as answered by the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier). I put my question to the appropriate Minister but I am not sure just which Minister is taking responsibility for the federal response to the PCB spill that occurred between Kenora and Ignace in northwestern Ontario. Transportation of dangerous goods legislation falls under the purview of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), but the Minister of the Environment released a news release yesterday reannouncing the coming into effect of the regulations under the transportation of dangerous goods legislation to which the Minister of Transport has referred the day before. We are not sure who is taking the responsibility for the federal response to this event.
I was just accused in committee by the Minister of Transport of not being patient and not waiting until all the facts were in. The fact of the matter is that we have to make decisions and evaluations on a day-to-day basis with respect to these kinds of events. 1 have been after the Government, not only with respect to the facts that we already know but with respect to what I consider to be its inadequate interest in finding out just what are the facts of the case.
What do we know? We know that the interprovincial transportation of dangerous goods is a federal responsibility, contrary to what the Minister of the Environment said the first day she was asked about this matter. On a personal level, we know of a Red Lake family comprised of a husband, a pregnant wife and two children that followed the truck for 25 kilometres, pulled it over because this stuff was spilling out onto them and were told by the driver that it was only mineral oil and that it could be cleaned up with some rags and gas and forgotten about. These people had to travel all the way to
Adjournment Debate
Winnipeg in a contaminated car before reading in the Winnipeg Free Press just what it was that had splashed all over their car. Their car has now been impounded and will be sent to Edmonton, I understand, for examination.
We know that the provincial hotline in Kenora advises those people who call with the suspicion that their cars may have been splashed with this substance to simply wash their cars down with water and paper towels and to put the paper towels in a plastic bag and take them to the dump. We know that the Quebec Government was led to believe by the company involved that the transformer was drained before shipment, and of course we now know that not to be the base at all.
We know that no one from the Department of Transport was on the scene for four days and that all that happened was that the federal Government made itself available to the Ontario Ministry of the Environment. No one was on the scene for four days, and even then no one from the Department of the Environment or the Dangerous Goods Division of the Department of Transport was present. The only person present was someone who did a very technical assessment of the transformer that leaked. These are the sorts of things we know. Another thing we know is that the RCMP has seized three shipments of improperly labelled soil samples that the Ontario Ministry of the Environment shipped on commercial airliners without the appropriate labelling.
I want to make clear what I have been saying all along, and that is that I think the Ontario Ministry of the Environment has really bungled this affair. I think the federal Government has taken a far too lackadaisical and uncritical attitude toward the Ontario Ministry of the Environment and the handling of this matter by the Ontario Government. They should not be so trusting of their colleagues in the Ontario Government. They should have had a desire to be on site to see what was going on. Indeed, the Government of Manitoba has already had two people on site for some time now because it wanted to know what was going on, for the sake of the people in that neighbouring province.
I suggested that there should be a moratorium on the further transportation of PCBs until all regulations pertaining to their transportation were in place. The Minister seems to be considering something of that nature, although every once in a while he tries to accuse me of wanting a total moratorium on the transportation of all hazardous substances. That is not what I suggested, at all. I was very specific in what 1 suggested.
I think there should be a public inquiry into the matter so that we can learn more about just what went on and ascertain facts in addition to the ones we already know. After that inquiry if we have one, or if we do not have one, in any event the book should be thrown at these people. The book should be thrown at these polluters, not just on the merits of this particular case, but so that a clear signal is sent out by the Government on behalf of the people indicating that Canadians will no longer tolerate polluters acting in the negligent way
