Adjournment Debate
they are in the habit of acting. We should draw the line and say that from here on in we will not tolerate this kind of behaviour. I think the Government could make an example of this particular company which would be useful for the environment and for the safety of the public for years to come.
Also I think the Minister should call for voluntary obedience under the regulations which will not come into effect until July
1.	Those regulations are public. They have been gazetted. I had a look at them this morning. They are available to the industry. Why does the Minister not call upon those companies that will be transporting dangerous substances to voluntarily obey the regulations until they come into force?
The Minister should also make clear just what the regulations will do and will not do. I think too much has been made of the regulations. Even if they were in effect, all that would have happened is that the speed of the response to the event and the accuracy of the response to the event would have been improved. The leak itself would not have been improved because regulations concerning containers in which dangerous substances are to be carried will not come into effect until even later. They have not even been gazetted. Let us not have the Government, particularly the Minister of the Environment, make too much of the regulations which are coming into effect.
Finally, again with respect to the regulations, we will not change all of this just by regulations or laws, although I think in this case the Government should seek every avenue possible to throw the book at whoever is determined to be responsible. We will change it when we finally get around to asking some very serious questions about the extent to which our whole economy depends upon dangerous substances. That is a point which I made earlier this week and one that I wanted to reiterate before hearing the reply of the Hon. Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Biais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY CHEMICAL SPILL-GOVERNMENT'S KNOWLEDGE OF INCIDENTS. (B) REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague has indicated that he does not know what are the areas of responsibilities of the various federal departments or how responsibilities are shared between the federal and provincial governments. I suggest that he should spend some time trying to find out how, in this country which is a confederation, responsibilities are shared between the federal and provincial governments.
The purpose of the federal legislation is to define common standards for all provinces, while provinces must take these standards and adapt them through legislation to their particular needs.
He told me that I should pressure the various provinces and companies into living up to the standards currently in force. That I have done and will continue to do. We have published a handbook which describes in minute details how to dispose of, transport and contain PCB. Most companies and several provinces have immediately agreed to apply these standards, so that, although the legislation has not come into force yet, Quebec is already applying these standards, and as soon as we
were advised that PCB would be transported, we immediately advised the Quebec Department of the Environment, as it was our federal responsibility to do, that a dangerous substance would be transported, asking that an inspector be sent to supervise the loading of the PCB.
My hon. friend said that four days elapsed before we responded. In fact, we were involved from the very beginning, in a manner consistent with our mandate and jurisdiction. Moreover, as soon as we learned that some PCB had been spilled on the highway, I contacted immediately Mr. Kells, the Ontario Minister and advised him that our expertise was at his disposal, with all the technical support he could need. It is indeed the responsibility of the province to act when such a crisis occurs. On the other hand, Mr. Kells knows that he can count on the assistance of the federal government and, as a matter of fact, he has asked us to contribute to put together a plan to dispose of the PCB waste. We indicated to him that we would help him implement this plan to dispose of all the waste and other substances which had to be removed because of the spill.
We are therefore very present and very much aware of PCB hazards. If the Hon. Member is so concerned about these hazards, and since the use of PCB has been banned since 1978, why did he not stand up in the House on several occasions to demand that provinces agree once and for all on a disposal site, something which has been delayed since 1978.

subtopic: ENERGY-NOTIFICATION OF ONTARIO PREMIER. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH ONTARIO PREMIER
ENERGY-NOTIFICATION OF ONTARIO PREMIER. (B) PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH ONTARIO PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 2, I raised a matter in this House with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) involving the energy accord between Canada and the western provinces. The issue today, Mr. Speaker, is not whether we are discussing the east versus the west or anything like that. What I want to know from this Government is how much will the consumers of this country have to pay-not in oil prices-in excess taxes? My question involved taxes. I want to ask this Government how much the consumers of this country will have to pay in excess taxes because of the oil deal which was signed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney)?
What we on this side of the House, and what the people of this country also want to know, is why was the Premier of the largest oil consuming province of this country, the Province of Ontario, not consulted by the Government? I see that the Parliamentary Secretary is taking notes. He is probably going to answer that the Minister of Energy of Ontario was consulted. That's fine, Mr. Speaker, but that is not what I am asking. I want to know very specifically when the Premier was consulted. I asked that question on April 2 and, of course, the Deputy Prime Minister answered a totally different question. He has a right to answer whatever he likes but, as you know, Mr. April 18, 1985

Speaker, he should at least answer the questions we are asking, which he did not do on that particular date.
According to estimates made by various people, the $1.3 billion lost by the federal Government in reduced revenues, if applied to the gasoline sales tax, would amount to an increase of 18 cents a gallon. You perhaps will recall, Mr. Speaker, that 18 cents a gallon is a figure which creates a certain adverse reaction amongst the Tories. Whenever they hear the words "18 cents a gallon" it really does something to them. But it is understandable. They were defeated the last time they tried to implement an 18 cent a gallon increase. What we want is the assurance that there will not be a disastrous 18 cent a gallon tax increase like the last time those Tories were in power. I am sure you recall vividly the disaster the last time they were in power.
If they can give us the assurance, and there is really only one means by which we can have that assurance, that there will not be a gasoline tax increase, I will be satisfied. But that is the only one way.
Two weeks from today there is a provincial election in the Province of Ontario. Why did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of this Government not table his Budget, including or excluding any disastrous tax increases that he proposes before the Ontario election? It is not a coincidence that this whole country has to wait for the political gain of those Tories who are not strong enough, who do not have the fortitude to bring in their Budget before the provincial election? I suspect that the Premier of Ontario probably tried to delay both the Western Accord and the Budget. However, there must have been a saw-off some place and they agreed they would delay the announcement of the Budget, because that would likely be a total disaster in terms of the vote-getting ability of the Premier of Ontario. It is being proved now during this election that the Premier's campaign is a total disaster anyway. However, we did not know that at the time, so the Premier of Ontario was not consulted before the oil-pricing agreement was signed. Afterwards he came to Ottawa, called an emergency meeting with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and pleaded his case.

Perhaps it was not an emergency, but let us say they called it in a hurry; on a few hours' notice they managed to have this meeting. Following the meeting we asked the Premier of Ontario what assurances he got. He replied, "well, I am told that we are going to do our best". Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Ontario was not consulted. He came to Ottawa in a hurry, came out empty handed, and this Government still refuses to bring in a Budget before the Ontario election.
We need to have the assurance that this Government is ready to put its money where its mouth is, and I challenge the

I listened to you without interrupting and I would expect the same courtesy. You have seven minutes, i have only three.
Listening to what he had to say, it is obvious he has sugar plums dancing through his mind. His imagination is running away with him. He should have stayed in the provincial House. If he wanted to run in the Liberal campaign for a seat, he should have stayed there instead of fighting the election here in the House of Commons, because it is just not working.
I can tell him that the Western Accord reduced taxes for the consumers of Ontario. It has removed those taxes which were piled on, one after the other, by the previous Liberal Government. The Western Accord is removing those taxes, deregulating the industry, oil prices are falling on the world market and so will they here. That is what deregulation is all about and that is what the Western Accord is all about. It is also about getting the energy sector going again.
In my riding of Brampton-Georgetown I have 53 companies who service the oil patch directly with products, and probably more if I did a little more investigating. But there are 53 which I have been able to find that feed the oil patch directly. So if it is going well with them, so it will with industry in Ontario. Jobs are being created in Ontario and that is very, very important. He asked if the Government consulted with the Government of Ontario.
